A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial repagination.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix G report original synthetic SSM experiments and clean-label poisoning experiments with S4 on CIFAR-10.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix I retain original synthetic results and report CIFAR-10 poisoning experiments with S4, Mamba-2, and LRU.

M1.justification: The real-world Gradient Matching adaptation changes: v4 Appendix J.3 partitions the poisoning budget between high-loss and remaining targets and optimizes poison groups against 50 targets each. The underlying SSM formulations and synthetic learning procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The synthetic tasks and CIFAR-10 dataset are retained. The real-world attack scenario shifts from disrupting selected test instances to attempting degradation across the entire CIFAR-10 test set; this changes the attack objective without adding a dataset or domain.

E2.justification: Both versions compare poisoned training with clean training and use adapted Gradient Matching for poisoning. Mamba-2 and LRU are additional attacked architectures, not competing poisoning methods; no comparison attack is added or removed.

E3.justification: The replacement real-world experiments use 20,000 clean training examples plus 10,000 poisons, versus v3's 45,000 clean examples and 500–5,000 poisons. Evaluation changes from targeted-instance accuracy to full-test accuracy and cross-entropy loss. v4 also adds model configurations and extends poisoned training to match clean training loss, subject to a 300-epoch cap.

E4.justification: v3 Table 2's variation in poison budgets and target counts is not retained. v4 Table 6 adds training-performance comparisons to examine whether deteriorating test performance accompanies poorer fitting. The existing dynamics, effective-rank, and gamma analyses in Figures 2–19 are retained.

E5.justification: v3 reports four-seed synthetic means without their standard deviations. v4 Tables 4 and 5 add those deviations, while the replacement real-world experiments report three-seed averages and deviations in Tables 7 and 8. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs for the retained synthetic experiments.

E6.justification: The six targeted S4 result rows in v3 Table 2 are replaced by full-test results for three architectures. v4 reports clean/poisoned accuracies of 78.8%/76.9% for S4, 77.8%/75.1% for Mamba-2, and 72.4%/68.3% for LRU, plus new training results in Table 6. These are different-setting results, not version-to-version performance changes. Synthetic Tables 1 and 3 retain their values.

T1.justification: v4 adds Theorem 2 in Appendix B and its proof in Appendix G, extending poisoning to arbitrary nonnegative training sequences ending in two zeros, with generalization-error lower bound 0.5−2/d. This goes substantially beyond v3 Appendix A's basis-vector and scaled-copy extensions, although the new guarantee permits large poison norms and concerns finite time rather than convergence.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims that cleanly labeled examples can disrupt SSM implicit bias and generalization, supported by a dynamical characterization and constructive poisoning theory. The expanded experiments support this existing contribution rather than establish a different core claim.

C2.justification: v4's conclusion proposes monitoring or penalizing gamma as possible, untested defenses. Appendix B adds large-norm and finite-time qualifications for Theorem 2, while omitting v3 Appendix A's separate discussion of remaining extension limitations, including non-diagonal models and large learning rates.

D1.justification: Compared with v3 Appendix H.2.4's brief implementation description and reliance on defaults, v4 Appendix J.3 and Table 19 provide a substantially fuller real-world workflow, additional implementation references, optimizer scheduling, training durations, and architecture-specific hyperparameters. The main code-access information and hardware disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds broader implicit-bias literature, including Saxe et al., Lampinen and Ganguli, and Alexander et al., and an overview sentence in related work. Its positioning relative to prior SSM and clean-label poisoning research remains substantially unchanged; citation-style conversion is separate.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 5 to Appendix A, experimental appendices are reorganized and renamed, and several introduction, theory-transition, experiment, and conclusion paragraphs are revised. Most exposition and the lengthy retained proofs preserve their structure and wording.

P2.justification: v4 adopts the NeurIPS layout, systematically changing typography, margins, author arrangement, and page flow. Table 2 is redesigned, uncertainty and training-performance tables are added, and implementation tables are consolidated near the end. All 19 figure objects are retained unchanged, although resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens empirical coverage, training-performance controls, uncertainty reporting, and reproducibility, but removes the earlier low-budget targeted-attack comparisons. More importantly, Appendix G bounds a rescaled loss equal to the original loss divided by c^2 without establishing the claimed tolerance for the original loss. This leaves the new theorem's low-training-loss guarantee unresolved. These competing gains and a material theoretical concern prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
